title: Liberty
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 23 of 40
content:
Liberty Prime was everything Danse loved about the Brotherhood made thirty feet tall and capable of throwing nuclear weapons.

He would object to that description.

It remained true.

The machine stood in pieces at Boston Airport while scribes and engineers crawled over it. Proctor Ingram shouted instructions from her power armor frame. Cables crossed the concrete. Crates of components arrived daily.

Danse was in his element.

“Look at this actuator assembly.”

“I am looking.”

“Pre-War engineering. Reinforced beyond any reasonable operational requirement.”

“You sound attracted to it.”

He looked at me in horror.

“To the engineering.”

“Sure.”

“Don’t make this strange.”

“You brought me here to admire a giant robot.”

“I brought you because Ingram requested additional hands.”

“And yet you’re giving me a tour.”

His ears reddened.

“Work.”

“Yes, Paladin.”

We spent the morning installing power conduits.

It was satisfying work. Clear problem, physical solution. Tighten the fitting. Test the line. Replace the cracked insulator. No ethics. No grief. No questions about what counted as human.

Danse relaxed around machines because machines did what they were built to do.

I wondered if that was part of the problem.

During lunch, we sat on a crate beneath Liberty Prime’s unfinished shadow.

Danse handed me half a sandwich.

“Did you steal this from Teagan?”

“I requisitioned it.”

“Without paperwork?”

“Eat.”

I did.

Across the bay, Ingram yelled at a scribe who had connected two cables incorrectly.

Danse smiled.

“You like her,” I said.

“She’s competent.”

“That is practically a love letter from you.”

He looked at me.

“I’ve kissed you.”

I nearly inhaled bread.

Danse realized what he had done.

His expression became priceless.

“You can’t just say things like that unexpectedly.”

“Why?”

“Because I have a respiratory system.”

He frowned.

“I don’t understand.”

“I know.”

That was half his charm and three-quarters of my problem.

After lunch, Quinlan arrived with a data slate.

He and Danse spoke quietly near the command table. I did not listen intentionally.

I heard my name—well, the designation the Brotherhood used for me—and then the words Institute records.

Danse looked over.

“What?” I asked when Quinlan left.

“Nothing relevant.”

“That sounded relevant.”

“Quinlan is cross-referencing data from recent operations.”

“About what?”

“Synth production. Personnel. Escapees.”

Danse’s voice went cold on the last word.

“Anything useful?”

“Not yet.”

He returned to work.

I watched him for a moment.

There are points in a life that become obvious only later.

At the time, Quinlan’s data slate was one more piece of Brotherhood business.

Later I would remember the exact angle of the light on Danse’s face.

That evening, the two of us remained at the airport after most crews left.

Liberty Prime towered above us in silence.

Danse sat on the concrete with his back against a crate.

I lowered myself beside him.

“Tired?”

“No.”

“Liar.”

He did not argue.

I rested my head on his shoulder.

After a moment his arm came around me.

“We shouldn’t do this here,” he said.

“Then move.”

He did not.

“Someone could see.”

“Terrifying.”

“This is a military installation.”

“You kissed me in a briefing room.”

“That was different.”

“How?”

He had no answer.

I smiled against his shoulder.

Above us, Liberty Prime waited to be rebuilt into exactly what the Brotherhood wanted him to be.

Danse’s thumb moved slowly along my sleeve.

“What?” he asked.

“Nothing.”

“You’re thinking.”

“I do that sometimes.”

“Dangerous habit.”

I looked up at him.

“Do you ever wonder who you’d be if the Brotherhood hadn’t found you?”

His expression changed.

“No.”

“Never?”

“I’d probably be dead.”

“That’s not an identity.”

“It’s enough of an answer.”

I let it go.

Danse leaned down and kissed my forehead.

The gesture was so spontaneous that we both froze afterward.

He looked mildly alarmed.

I smiled.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“Don’t.”

“You’re adorable.”

“I am a Brotherhood paladin.”

“Both things can be true.”

He groaned.

Liberty Prime remained silent.

I decided not to ask the robot for support.

Two days later Liberty Prime’s right hand moved for the first time.

The entire work bay stopped.

Hydraulics groaned. Servos engaged. Five enormous metal fingers curled into a fist with slow mechanical certainty.

The scribes cheered.

Danse looked delighted.

Not politely pleased. Delighted.

I had seen him survive explosions with less visible emotion.

“Look at that response time,” he said.

“I am looking.”

“Nearly instantaneous considering the mass.”

“You want to marry the robot.”

He turned on me.

“We established this.”

“We established that you’re attracted to the engineering.”

“That sentence is worse.”

Ingram rolled past us in her power armor frame.

“Ignore them, Danse. Prime’s already taken.”

He stared at her.

I had to sit down.

The work crew laughed loud enough to echo through the airport.

Danse endured it with the dignity of a man under artillery fire.

Later, when the bay emptied, he found me tightening a conduit clamp and stood beside me in silence.

“You enjoyed that.”

“Immensely.”

“I expect better from you.”

“No, you don’t.”

His mouth twitched.

Then his gaze lifted toward Prime.

“I used to hear stories about him at the Citadel.”

“Liberty Prime?”

“Yes. The Brotherhood recovered and repaired him years ago. For younger soldiers, he was…”

Danse searched for the word.

“Proof.”

“Of what?”

“That the old world had not destroyed everything worth preserving.”

The answer was more personal than I expected.

I set down the wrench.

“You really do love this stuff.”

“Technology?”

“The idea that broken things can be put back together.”

Danse went still.

I realized what I had said only after it landed.

Above us, Liberty Prime stood in pieces, cables hanging from his chest, one newly functional hand resting at his side.

Danse looked away.

“Repair has limits.”

“Sure.”

“Some damage is irreversible.”

“Yes.”

“And some things should not be rebuilt.”

There it was—the doctrine returning, neat and hard-edged.

I leaned back against the workbench.

“How do you decide?”

“By whether the thing is dangerous.”

“Prime is a nuclear weapon with legs.”

“He is under Brotherhood control.”

“That is exactly the kind of sentence that gives me hives.”

Danse sighed.

“You know what I mean.”

“I do. I’m just not sure control is the same thing as safety.”

He looked at me.

Another philosophical argument waiting to happen.

Instead he said, “You worry too much.”

I laughed.

“That from you?”

He considered the hypocrisy.

“Fair.”

We returned to the conduit.

Later, Proctor Ingram ran Liberty Prime through a partial actuator test.

The machine’s enormous arm lifted six inches and locked with a hydraulic boom that echoed across the airport.

Everyone around us cheered.

Danse did too.

Not loudly. One sharp exhale and a grin he failed to hide.

I looked at him instead of the robot.

“What?” he asked.

“You’re happy.”

“Prime represents a significant engineering achievement.”

“Happy.”

“He could change the strategic balance of the entire Commonwealth.”

“Very happy.”

Danse crossed his arms.

“You are determined to make enthusiasm embarrassing.”

“No. I like seeing you want something.”

That stopped him.

The grin faded into something more vulnerable.

“I want the Institute stopped.”

“I know.”

“That is not selfish.”

“I didn’t say it had to be.”

He looked back at Liberty Prime.

The Brotherhood gave Danse permission to want things when they could be called objectives. Victory. Technology. Security. Useful wants.

Personal wants still seemed like contraband.

I touched his elbow.

“What would you do if we had an entire day with no assignment?”

“Equipment maintenance.”

“That is an assignment you invented.”

He thought harder.

“Sleep.”

“Better.”

“Possibly read.”

“What?”

“Technical manuals.”

I groaned.

Danse smiled. “You asked.”

“I am going to find you a terrible novel.”

“That sounds like a threat.”

“It is.”

He looked almost curious despite himself.

Ingram eventually shouted at us to stop distracting her technicians and either work or leave.

Danse chose work.

Of course he did.

He crawled beneath a conduit housing with me and spent twenty minutes explaining why Prime’s cabling had redundant shielding. I understood perhaps half of it.

He noticed.

“You’re not listening.”

“I’m listening to you.”

“That is not the same as understanding.”

“No.”

He slid out far enough to look at me.

“You like hearing me talk about this.”

It was not really a question.

“Yes.”

The realization embarrassed him more effectively than any teasing could have.

He disappeared under the housing again.

“Hand me the three-eighths driver.”

I smiled and did.

A few minutes later Danse handed me a tool before I asked for it.

I handed him a connector before he asked for that.

We worked almost wordlessly, anticipating each other’s movements.

That was becoming our most comfortable language.

At one point his shoulder brushed mine.

Neither of us moved away.

“Danse?”

“Yes?”

“You know you’re allowed to like things that aren’t useful.”

He glanced at me.

“Such as?”

“Music. Bad jokes. sitting somewhere with no tactical value. Me.”

His expression softened.

“You’re useful.”

I stared.

He held the serious face for two seconds before it broke.

I shoved his shoulder.

“You absolute bastard.”

He laughed.

The sound rang up into the unfinished machine above us.

For once, Danse had made the joke first.

I decided that counted as a successful repair too.
